blocks.text: I add that there is no apparent reason why the hen, or the attagen, or the urogallus [col. 348] or tetraon should be counted among the unclean birds. Indeed, everyone knows that the use of the hen was permitted to the Jews. And you may read the same about the attagen in Aristeas, a spurious author, to be sure, but nevertheless a Jewish one and very old, since he is cited by Josephus as a genuine writer. His words are: Τῶν γὰρ πτηνῶν οἷς χρώμεθα πάντα ἥμερα καθέστηκε. διαφέρει καθαρότητι, πυροῖς καὶ ὀσπρίοις χρώμενα πρὸς τὴν τροφήν· οἷον περιστεραὶ, τρυγόνες, ἀτταγαὶ, πέρδικες, ἔτι χῆνες, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ὅσα τοιαῦτα. [Tōn gar ptēnōn hois chrōmetha panta hēmera kathestēke. diapherei katharotēti, pyrois kai ospriois chrōmena pros tēn trophēn; hoion peristerai, trygones, attagai, perdikes, eti chēnes, kai ta alla hosa toiauta.] The birds that we use are all tame; they excel in cleanness and are fed on wheat and pulses, such as doves, turtledoves, attagens, partridges, geese too, and others of that kind. (Instead of ἀτταγαὶ [attagai], attagens, ἀττακοὶ [attakoi] is wrongly read, which is a kind of locust, Levit. XI, 22.) The hen and the attagen, therefore, were permitted to the Jews, and there appears to be no reason why they should have been forbidden to them. But in the case of the hoopoe the matter is clear, since it is a most filthy bird, which builds its nest out of dung and feeds on the most fetid things. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 15: Ὁ δὲ ἔποψ τὴν νεοττίαν μάλιστα ποιεῖται ἐκ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης κόπρου. [Ho de epops tēn neottian malista poieitai ek tēs anthrōpinēs koprou.] The hoopoe makes its nest chiefly out of human excrement. Aelian, History, book 3, [III, 114] chapter 26: Οἱ δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ πηλοῦ χρίουσι τὴν καλιὰν, ἀποπάτημα ἀνθρώπου περιβαλόντες, τῇ δυσωδίᾳ τε καὶ κακοσμίᾳ ἀνείργοντες καὶ ἀναστέλλοντες τὸ ζῶον τὸ ἑαυτοῖς πολέμιον· [Hoi de anti tou pēlou chriousi tēn kalian, apopatēma anthrōpou peribalontes, tē dysōdia te kai kakosmia aneirgontes kai anastellontes to zōon to heautois polemion;] Instead of mud, they plaster their nest with human excrement, warding off and repelling by the stench and foul smell any animal hostile to them. Pliny, book 10, chapter 29: A bird otherwise filthy in its feeding. Cyril, book 3, On Adoration: Εἶδος δὲ τοῦτο στρουθίου τὰ τῶν τελμάτων ἀεὶ δυσωδέστατα περιθέοντος, καὶ τὰ ἐκ βορβόρου καὶ ἀκαθαρσίας συλλέγοντος εἰς τροφήν· [Eidos de touto strouthiou ta tōn telmatōn aei dysōdestata peritheontos, kai ta ek borborou kai akatharsias syllegontos eis trophēn;] It is a kind of little bird that constantly flies about the most fetid parts of marshes and seeks its food from mire and filth. And on Zechariah, volume 3: Φιλοβόρβορον (ἐστὶ) καὶ κοπροβόρον καὶ ταῖς σκωλήκων ἀγέλαις ἀγρίως ἐπιμαινόμενον, καὶ τροφὴν ἀεὶ ποιεῖσθαι κατειθισμένον τὴν ἐσχάτην ἀκαθαρσίαν· [Philoborboron (esti) kai koproboron kai tais skōlēkōn agelais agriōs epimainomenon, kai trophēn aei poieisthai kateithismenon tēn eschatēn akatharsian;] It is a bird that delights in mire, feeds on dung, rages fiercely against swarms of worms, and is accustomed to take all the most unclean things as food. And in Homily 10 On the Paschal Feasts: Ἀκάθαρτον γὰρ τὸ στρουθίον, φημὶ δὴ τὸν ἔποπα, σκωλήκων τε καὶ περισσευμάτων τῶν ἀπὸ γαστρὸς ὅτι μάλιστα βορόν· [Akatharton gar to strouthion, phēmi dē ton epopa, skōlēkōn te kai perisseumatōn tōn apo gastros hoti malista boron;] The hoopoe, I say, is an unclean little bird, which delights above all in feeding on worms and the excrements of the belly. Jerome on Zechariah ch. 5: They call it Ἔποπα [Epopa] from the fact that it settles on human excrement. They say it is a most filthy bird, always dwelling in tombs, always in human dung. Finally, it is also said to make its nest from it, and to feed its young on the little worms of rotting dung. Hence Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 7: The Greeks call it upupa, because it settles on human excrement and feeds on stinking dung, a most filthy bird ^{(2)}. Yet I by no means approve this derivation of the Greek name. I prefer to agree with Varro, who derives the name upupa from its call. For it seems constantly to repeat epop or upup. Hence it is told in the myths that Tereus, changed into a hoopoe, cried ποῦ; ποῦ; [pou? pou?] where? where?, as pursuers do, when he was pursuing Procne and Philomela. And the Arabic name of the hoopoe, هدهد [hudhud] hudhud, seems to belong to the same origin. For the calls of birds, since they are not articulate, can be rendered in various ways.

Close to the Hebrew דוכיפת dukiphath is the Egyptian KUKUPHA, which means the hoopoe. Hence in the Coptic Lexicon ΚΟΥΚΟΥΦᾺ [koukoupha] is rendered in Arabic by الهدهد [al-hudhud] alhudhud, that is, the hoopoe. The Syriac ܩܝܩܘܦܐ kikupha too [III, 115] is so explained in Ferrarius's Syriac Lexicon. And that the hoopoe is meant by the name cucupha is clear from these words of Horapollo, book 1, chapter 52: Εὐχαριστίαν γράφοντες (Αἰγύπτιοι) κουκουφὰν ζωγραφοῦσι, διότι τοῦτο μόνον τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων, ἐπειδὰν ὑπὸ τῶν γονέων ἐκτραφῇ, γηράσασιν αὐτοῖς, τὴν [col. 349] αὐτὴν ἀνταποδίδωσι χάριν. [Eucharistian graphontes (Aigyptioi) koukouphan zōgraphousi, dioti touto monon tōn alogōn zōōn, epeidan hypo tōn goneōn ektraphē, gērasasin autois, tēn autēn antapodidōsi charin.] When they signify gratitude, they (the Egyptians) paint a cucupha, because this alone of the dumb animals, after it has been reared by its parents, repays them the same kindness when they are worn out with age. For the Egyptians hold hoopoes in honour, as Aelian testifies, History, book 10, chapter 16, because they are πρὸς τοὺς γειναμένους εὐσεβεῖς [pros tous geinamenous eusebeis], dutiful towards their parents.
